newsitem.title: USA: Cruise lines fine tune Panama Canal bookings plan.
newsitem.headline: Cruise lines fine tune Panama Canal bookings plan.

text.p: The cruise line industry has successfully led efforts to keep a lid on reservation fees associated with crossing the Panama Canal during peak congestion, fine tuning a new booking scheme the Panama Canal Commission began testing in April.

Under the scheme, both commercial shippers and cruise liners who had reserved well ahead of time found booking fees went up nearly threefold if they arrived at times of "condition three" congestion when the backlog of ships awaiting transit rises to at least 90 ships.

Cruise liners, faced not only with paying for canal reservations for the first time ever but paying some of the highest transit tolls of any ships crossing the canal, saw the trebling scheme unfair and unacceptable.
"I have heard that we raised many of the issues," said John Overstreet, spokesman at the International Council of Cruise Lines, a Washington, D.C.-based trade group.
"Our argument to these guys was the cruise industry already pays the highest tolls in the industry," Overstreet said.
Transit fees are paid by all canal users, whereas booking or reservation fees are limited to users who choose to reserve passage ahead of time for commercial reasons.

Transit fees are levied based on a complex calculation of a ship's internal usable space, and given the somewhat bulbous shape of many modern cruise liners, cruise ship transit tolls often top the list at amounts as high as $150,000 per passage.
Richard Wainio, director of the Panama Canal Commission's office of executive planning in Panama, acknowledged cruise liner operators were among the most vocal protesters.

He said it appeared they were not willing to accept both the advent of booking fees and the trebling component of the new rules. But he stressed severe congestion that triggers the higher fees typically occurs only during periods of canal maintenance.
"We listened and we're making changes that will make the cruise lines, if not happy, then certainly more satisfied than they would have been without them," Wainio said.

Wainio said the objections quickly came to the fore the very day testing of the new scheme began in April when a tugboat sank in the canal. The sinking shut one of the lanes, quickly backing up traffic to "condition three" congestion and triggering the higher booking fee scheme.
Under such conditions, booking fees for most ships balloon to about $0.69 per tonne (Panama Canal/Universal Measurement System), from the $0.26 per tonne charged for transit during normal conditions.
"If there's a silver lining to the tug sinking, it's that it certainly stress-tested the new rules and highlighted the problems," Wainio said. "As a result, changes are being made."
He said the changes will not be made until after the end of the test period, which the commission recently extended until the end of September.

"We understand that some changes will be made at the end of the test period, and that some of these will be to honor the original booking price," said a shipping source in Panama who requested anonymity.

Wainio said testing of the new booking scheme and other changes was launched in April for a number of reasons -- most noteworthy among them to address customer requests for changes to the booking system and to more efficiently control time sensitive bookings.
Under the proposed new system, 21 of the canal's 40 per day transit capacity can be reserved ahead of time, with that number dropping to 12 during condition three congestion.
Under the previous system, the maximum number of bookings in normal conditions was 16 and the booking system was entirely abandoned in times of severe congestion, Wainio said.
He said the canal can handle about 40 ships per day, but is averaging just 37 so far this year.
The new system brings cruise liners into the booking fold for the first time, though they will not have to pay for their reservation until the changes are finalized in the autumn.
Previously, they had no obligation to book and were given top priority in any queue, regardless of its length.
Wainio stressed cruise lines will still be given priority in transiting, since keeping cruising vacationers on hold at the mouth of the canal for too long is unacceptable.
He said under the new system, cruise ships receive three booking slots per day as long as they are reserved between 365 and 21 days before transit.
"In our industry, we have to go through the canal when we say we'll go through," the Cruise Council's Overstreet said.
((-- New York Energy Desk 1 212 859 1633))
